item.title: The Third of May 1808
item.lesson: On May 2, 1808, Madrid rose against Napoleon's occupying army; on May 3, French firing squads worked through the night executing hundreds. Six years later, after the French were expelled, Goya asked the restored Spanish government to let him commemorate the uprising — and delivered something no one had ever painted. War art had always meant heroes: generals on horses, noble deaths. Goya paints the mechanics of slaughter instead. The firing squad is a faceless machine, a single many-legged organism of greatcoats and rifles; the victims are peasants, one already face-down in his own blood. At the center, lit by a paper lantern, a man in a white shirt throws his arms wide — the pose of crucifixion, given to an anonymous laborer. There is no glory anywhere in the frame, only before and after. Manet copied its structure; Picasso had it in his bones when he painted Guernica. Modern war painting, and arguably modern political art, starts here.
item.lookFor: Look at the white-shirted man's right palm: it bears a wound like a stigma. Then notice the lantern — the only light source — sits with the executioners. Illumination belongs to the killers; Goya makes light itself complicit.
